rv.q: Neilson’s expertly acted production is one long sleight of hand.

’The Tell-Tale Heart’ is gross. Like, really gross. Like we’re talking hacked-limbs, ruptured-organs gross. I am trying to eat my breakfast while writing this review, and it is proving a bit ‘challenging’, is how gross it is. It’s also the National Theatre’s Christmas show!!
Neilson does Poe — and it’s mightily enjoyable.
It's a deft, macabre turn by Neilson, who also directs.
Lawrance reminds us why she is one of the best young actresses around, allowing Celeste’s inner demons to strain behind every seemingly laid-back, liberal sentence.
Yet while there's plenty of twisted humour, it feels like a cheeky sketch that's been extended beyond its ideal length.

The good-natured grotesquerie is handled with ease by a pitch-perfect cast, all of whom play the intended overripeness of the writing with po-faced (you'll forgive the adjective) precision: I shan't soon forget the conviction with which Carlyle employs a second-act simile designed to make your maiden aunt blanch.
It's all skilfully done, funny and frightening by turns.

In Act 1 I'd say Neilson proves himself Poe's equal. In Act 2 I wished he'd learnt from his predecessors, brevity and economy to hone something genuinely short, sharp and shocking rather than something that out stays its welcome.
It’s hard to see how this dramatic mutant will win an audience.
An excellent cast and a great deal of theatre jiggery-pokery (projection, clever lighting and sound) produce some really quite unsettling moments.

cn.t: Critics largely praise Neilson's darkly comic Poe adaptation for its gleeful grotesquerie, though some find the expanded plot overreaches. Strong performances win favor, but a divisive outlier drags the otherwise positive reception.
